content: 1. Patients with steatosis, lipodystrophy, or lipatrophy, particularly those with a BMI greater than 25 or a body weight exceeding 75 kg, and those with prolonged exposure to nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), should consider substitution with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or abacavir (ABC). 2. Dolutegravir (DTG) may cause hepatotoxicity and hypersensitivity reactions. In cases of hepatitis B or C coinfection or pre-existing liver disease, caution is advised. If DTG is used as part of first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) and hypersensitivity reactions occur, substitution with another therapeutic class, such as efavirenz (EFV) or boosted protease inhibitors (PIs), is recommended. 3. Darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) can lead to hepatotoxicity, especially in individuals with underlying liver disease, hepatitis B or C coinfection, or concurrent use of hepatotoxic drugs. Substitution with atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r) or lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) is suggested. In third-line ART, options for substitution may be limited. 4. Efavirenz (EFV) is associated with persistent central nervous system (CNS) toxicity, including dizziness, insomnia, abnormal dreams, anxiety, depression, or mental confusion. For CNS symptoms, dosing at nighttime is recommended. If symptoms persist, consider using a lower dose of EFV (400 mg/day) or substituting with nevirapine (NVP) or an integrase inhibitor like DTG. 5. Severe hepatotoxicity or hypersensitivity reactions to EFV warrant substitution with another therapeutic class, such as integrase inhibitors or boosted PIs. EFV may also cause gynecomastia, though the risk factors are unknown. Substitution with NVP or another therapeutic class is recommended in such cases. 6. Etravirine (ETV) can cause severe skin and hypersensitivity reactions. In such cases, substitution with another therapeutic class, such as integrase inhibitors or boosted PIs, is advised. 7. Lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) may lead to electrocardiographic abnormalities, including PR and QRS interval prolongation or torsades de pointes, particularly in individuals with pre-existing conduction system disease or those on concomitant drugs that prolong these intervals. Use with caution in such patients. LPV/r is also associated with hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, dyslipidemia, and diarrhea. Substitution with ATV/r, DRV/r, or integrase inhibitors is recommended in cases of toxicity. 8. Nevirapine (NVP) can cause hepatotoxicity, severe skin rash, and hypersensitivity reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Risk factors include underlying liver disease, hepatitis B or C coinfection, and high baseline CD4 cell counts (>250 cells/mm³ in women or >400 cells/mm³ in men). For mild hepatotoxicity, substitution with EFV is recommended. For severe hepatotoxicity or hypersensitivity, substitution with integrase inhibitors or boosted PIs is advised. 9. Raltegravir (RAL) is associated with rhabdomyolysis, myopathy, and myalgia, particularly when used with other drugs that increase the risk of these conditions, such as statins. Substitution with etravirine or boosted PIs is recommended in such cases. 10. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) is linked to renal toxicity, characterized by proximal tubular cell dysfunction, acute kidney injury, or chronic kidney disease, as well as bone mineral density loss. Risk factors include low body weight (<50 kg), untreated hypertension or diabetes, and concurrent use of nephrotoxic drugs. TDF should not be initiated in individuals with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <50 mL/min, uncontrolled hypertension, or renal failure. Substitution with zidovudine (AZT) or ABC is recommended in such cases. 11. Monitoring for TDF toxicity should include renal function tests, such as serum creatinine and eGFR, when available. Routine blood pressure monitoring is also advised. In high-risk individuals, laboratory monitoring is recommended to detect and limit further renal impairment. 12. Abacavir (ABC) is associated with hypersensitivity reactions (HSR), particularly in individuals with the HLA-B5701 allele. Screening for this allele is recommended before initiating ABC therapy. ABC has also been linked to an increased risk of myocardial infarction in adults. Substitution with another therapeutic class is advised in cases of toxicity. 13. Integrase inhibitors, such as dolutegravir (DTG) and raltegravir (RAL), generally have favorable safety profiles with low potential for drug interactions. However, DTG may cause mild to moderate nausea, headache, and diarrhea, as well as abnormal liver function in patients with hepatitis B or C coinfection. RAL is associated with rare severe adverse reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and rhabdomyolysis. 14. In children and adolescents, the toxicity profiles of TDF, RAL, and other antiretroviral drugs are similar to those observed in adults. However, careful growth monitoring and accurate dosing are critical to minimize toxicity. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry testing is not widely available, but monitoring for bone mineral density loss is recommended when possible. 15. Limited data are available on the use of integrase inhibitors in pregnant or breastfeeding women. Further research is needed to establish their safety profiles in these populations.
